source.title: Penalizing Gradient Norm for Efficiently Improving Generalization in Deep Learning
source.authors: Yang Zhao; Hao Zhang; Xiuyuan Hu

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text includes the paper and appendix.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a different explicit regularization method improves held-out image-classification performance, compared with standard training and SAM. It does not test the specific behaviors named in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-error results for gradient-norm penalty training and the standard and SAM baselines. Its cited results about other studies are not included as rows. The parameter sweeps in Figure 2 are used to select hyperparameters; only their described conclusions are noted in the excerpts.
record.test_reason: The study uses the premise that flatter minima generalize better to motivate a gradient-norm penalty and reports its method's test errors against SGD and SAM. It tests none of V1–V8. In particular, gradient norm and test error do not measure V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, training–test gaps, or ranking against alternative measures.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the authors' conclusion: they present an efficiently approximated gradient-norm penalty, describe SAM as its special case, and claim improved CIFAR and ImageNet performance with appropriate tuning. Qualify any suggestion of universal superiority: standard SGD performs best for original VGG16 on CIFAR-100 with cutout, and excessive penalty strength harms performance.
record.recipe_differences: Adds a gradient-norm penalty, implemented with a first-order approximation; compares the proposed scheme with standard SGD and SAM. The paper uses CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet classifiers, not the random-label memorization or other interventions in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies with balance coefficient α, approximation scalar r, dataset, architecture, and augmentation. The paper reports best performance around α=0.7 or 0.8 for the parameter study; for α>1, testing error rises as the gradient norm rapidly drops. Negative α trials fail to converge.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed gradient-norm penalty lowers test error relative to standard training in most recorded settings and relative to SAM in all recorded settings. Original VGG16 on CIFAR-100 with cutout is an exception against standard training: 27.07% versus 26.98%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A suitably tuned first-order gradient-norm penalty can improve image-classification test performance relative to standard SGD and SAM, with architecture- and recipe-dependent gains.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4.1 and Figure 3 report that coefficients above one rapidly suppress gradient norm while test error rises; negative coefficients fail to converge. These measure sensitivity to the proposed penalty, not magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stronger gradient-norm suppression does not necessarily improve test performance; penalty strength requires tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 162, 2022
record.problems: No training errors or train-test gaps are reported, so the table outcomes do not measure gap changes directly. The original VGG16 results use the best training case, possibly after more than five trials and not strictly following the greedy strategy. PyramidNet uses three seeds; other table cases use five. ImageNet uses only three seeds and a 100-epoch schedule. The paper says SAM failures under cutout led to lowering the learning rate for stability.
record.rows_left_out: Rows for WideResNet-SS 2×96, ViT-S16, and additional ViT-TI16/VGG16-BN conditions are omitted due to the 60-row cap. Their values appear in Table 1 for WideResNet-SS and Tables 2–3 for ViT; VGG16-BN values are in Table 1. Priority was given to keeping rows for the displayed model and both augmentation conditions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization under matching recipes, and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Width variation beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity. ViTs are not the specified fully connected comparator.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; SAM is not an adaptive optimizer comparison of this kind.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Controlled dropout addition or removal, training-set-size dependence, and joint dropout/weight-decay removal.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test gaps at comparable training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized training examples versus matched random removal and subsequent test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: All 60 numerical rows match the supplied tables, but they report method performance outside V1–V8 and should not serve as claim-test rows. Their cannot_determine states concern applicability to these versions, not readability of the values. No omitted result tests a listed version. The rows_left_out description is inaccurate about Table 1: all displayed WideResNet-SS and VGG16-BN conditions are already recorded; ImageNet Table 4 is omitted without being declared there.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under differing tuning.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects, including interactions with training set size and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurement and its correlation with training-test gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
